challenges.name: circular-import-quiz
challenges.title: Is the import cycle gone?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the refund refactor: what tsc and madge say about the orders/payments cycle, and the assistant's second attempt that loads orders inside refund().

questions.explanation: True. TypeScript checks types, not load order: the type of orderRepository is OrderRepository, so new RefundService(orderRepository) type-checks. At runtime the server loads orders first; orders starts loading payments before its own orderRepository line has run, payments asks for orders, gets a module that is not finished yet, and RefundService keeps undefined. tsc has no rule for that, which is why teams add madge --circular, the import/no-cycle rule of eslint-plugin-import or a dependency-cruiser no-circular rule to CI. The misconception is that a clean tsc run means every import holds a value; types describe what a value should be, not whether the module that exports it has finished loading.

False. payments still needs orders and orders still needs payments; the require only moved from load time to call time. By the time refund runs, orders has finished loading, so the crash goes away - until someone uses orders at the top of payments again, or a test or a script loads payments first. The dependency still points the wrong way (payments, the lower-level module, knows about orders), and the two modules still cannot be built, tested or extracted separately. The fixes remove the edge: move what both need (the order records) into a third module, or give payments a small port it receives from outside, or keep refund orchestration in orders. The misconception is that a cycle is a load-time problem only; the crash was the symptom, the two-way dependency is the cause.

challenges.name: spot-the-ai-mistake-circular-import
challenges.title: Spot the AI Mistake: a refactor with a circular import
challenges.description: An AI assistant was asked: "Move the refund logic out of the orders module into payments, where the rest of the money code lives. The order page must keep showing 'refundable until <date>'." It moved refund() into payments, and to find the order and mark it refunded, payments now loads orders - while orders already loads payments to charge and to show the deadline. Placing and showing orders still work, so the review passed. Since the release every refund fails with a TypeError, and support refunds learners by hand. The modules are objects registered with define() on a tiny module loader in the starter that behaves like CommonJS require(): a module that loads another module still in the middle of loading gets undefined, and every load() a module makes is recorded in an import graph. Fix the modules so that refunds work and the import graph has no cycle: payments.refund(orderId, today) keeps its signature and its rules (unknown_order, already_refunded, window_closed after paid-on date + 14 days, otherwise the order becomes refunded and the result carries a new refund id re_<n> and the amount), and orders keeps placeOrder, getOrder, markRefunded and describe. You may add modules with define() and the Modules interface. The test runner reads a list of actions (place, show, refund, graph) from stdin, loads orders and then payments like the app entry, and prints one line per action (only a summary line for more than 40 actions); the graph action prints "no import cycle" or the graph with the cycle it found. Do not change the loader, the shared types or the test runner. The public tests pass on the assistant's code; the hidden tests refund orders and check the import graph.
hints: Run your code with the input [{"do":"graph"}]. Which module loads which, and when payments runs `load("orders")`, has orders finished loading yet?

Look at what payments actually needs from orders: only getOrder and markRefunded, which work on the list of orders. Where could that list live so that both orders and payments can use it without either one loading the other?

A similar cycle elsewhere: progress loads catalog to read lesson counts, and catalog loads progress to show "3 of 12 lessons done". Moving the lesson counts into a third module, lessons, that imports nothing, turns progress -> catalog -> progress into progress -> lessons and catalog -> lessons, catalog -> progress. Loading the other module inside a function instead of at the top would only hide the cycle.
